Welcome—I'm so glad you're here.
Have you ever looked back on your childhood and felt that familiar mix of laughter and longing?
Together, we're about to set off on a journey where nostalgia and humor blend beautifully, turning everyday moments into something unforgettable.
Through the eyes of a young boy in 1950s Des Moines, Bill Bryson’s The Life and Times of the Thunderbolt Kid sweeps us into a world where optimism and innocence seem to paint every memory in brighter colors.
Imagine seeing your hometown not just as it was, but as an endless playground—filled with comic books, brand-new televisions, and the first taste of suburban adventure.
What if you could see the world as a kid who truly believes he's a superhero, navigating the delightful chaos of family life and the wonders of a rapidly changing America?
As we step into this story, you'll meet quirky neighbors, relive the rituals of growing up, and feel the tug of that universal longing for excitement and discovery.
But there’s more beneath the mischief and laughter—a deeper look at a country finding its way, where small-town comforts rub elbows with big changes on the horizon.
Bryson's storytelling wraps us in warmth and wit, reminding us how magical the ordinary can be—and how, even as times change, the spirit of adventure and imagination never really fades.
So, let’s explore together. Get ready to rediscover the joys, the absurdities, and the heart of mid-century America.

Chapter 1: Growing Up in a World of Possibility and Wonder
You know, there’s a special kind of magic about childhood—especially when the world around you feels safe, but still full of surprise and adventure.
Right after World War II, there was this wave of optimism rolling through America. If you were growing up in a place like Des Moines, Iowa, every day felt like a mix of the ordinary and the extraordinary. The streets were lined with neat little houses, neighbors waved hello, and there was always this feeling in the air—like something new and exciting might show up at any moment.
Imagine being a kid in that world. Suddenly, everything's a playground. The corner grocery store? It’s not just for bread and milk—it’s where you might find a secret stash of candy, the latest comic book, or maybe even sneak a forbidden treat. Movie theaters, with their glowing signs, let you step into faraway worlds and root for heroes you’d never meet in real life. Even the living room at home, with the radio humming or a black-and-white TV flickering, became a place for dreams and laughter.
At the heart of it all was family. Picture a dad who worked at the newspaper—curious, a little dry with his humor, but always finding joy in small, everyday things. He’d read the paper, tinker with whatever gadgets he could find, and always had a story or two ready for the dinner table. And mom? She kept everything running smoothly, practical but warm, always balancing saving money with making life just a little more fun. Even the simplest meal felt special when she was in charge, and her gentle jokes could soften any rough day.
For a kid back then, the days were wide open. No cell phones. No one watching your every move. You’d grab your bike or just your imagination and set off—exploring the neighborhood, making up games, and maybe pushing the boundaries a bit. The local park turned into a kingdom. The backyard? That was your science lab, where you ran experiments that were sometimes smart, sometimes... a little mischievous. Friends would gather for spontaneous baseball games, and their laughter would echo down the street.
But even with all that freedom, there was this quiet sense that the world you knew was pretty unique. The postwar boom meant families had more, but it also made everything feel a little bit the same. Most folks lived in similar houses, drove the same kinds of cars, and everyone tuned in to the same TV shows at night. There was comfort in that sameness, but sometimes it made you crave something a little different, a little more exciting.
That’s where imagination really kicked in. One kid, for example, dreamed up his own superhero—the Thunderbolt Kid. Armed with nothing but a towel-cape and a wild imagination, he could zap away boredom, turn chores into daring missions, and make even the dullest day feel like an adventure. For him, Thunderbolt Kid wasn’t just pretend—it was a way to handle the ups and downs of growing up, to feel a little stronger, a little more in control.
Thinking back, it’s easy to see how those days shaped everyone who lived through them. The 1950s might seem innocent now, but there were plenty of contradictions bubbling underneath. The world outside looked steady, but big changes were just around the corner—social shifts that would shake everything up. Still, for that kid in Des Moines, the world felt wide open, packed with possibilities. Anything could happen—and honestly, it usually did.

Let’s step right into Chapter 2: Family Life, Eccentricities, and the Comforts of Home.
Picture a home in the 1950s. It wasn’t just a place where you slept, was it? Back then, home was the heart of everything. The kitchen table? That was command central. It’s where families shared meals, tackled homework, and sometimes, hashed out those spirited debates that only made you closer.
Move over to the living room, and you’d find a worn-out sofa and a TV that flickered on and off—almost like it had a mind of its own. That little stage set the scene for both laughter and, let’s be honest, the occasional family drama. Every family had its own unique rhythm—its special rules, and yes, a collection of oddball habits that were just part of the package.
In one household, the dad’s job at the local newspaper set the tone for daily life. He was out the door before sunrise and back in the evening, always with a story or two from the newsroom. His humor? It was dry, sometimes so absurd you couldn’t help but laugh. He loved sharing the weirdest facts and pulling off gentle pranks—just enough to keep everyone on their toes.
And gadgets? Oh, he couldn’t resist. Radios, toasters, those early TV sets—if it promised to make life easier or more interesting, it found a place in the house. Of course, each gadget had its own personality—quirks, malfunctions, and all.
Now, let’s not forget Mom. She was the glue that held everything together. Managing the household budget with an eagle eye, she somehow found a way to stretch every dollar. Her cooking might’ve been simple, but it always hit the spot. And when it came to leftovers, she could magic up something new and delicious without breaking a sweat. She handled chaos with a steady calm, smiling even when things got a little wild.
Life at home was this perfect blend of routine and surprise. Siblings? Sure, they argued over chores or who got to pick the TV show, but when it mattered, they always teamed up—especially if parental discipline was looming.
There were unspoken rules everyone knew by heart. Who got the last slice of pie? How long was too long in the bathroom? What counted as a reasonable bedtime? Even the family car—sturdy, a little temperamental—was a character in its own right. It sparked both pride and frustration. Road trips became their own kind of adventure, full of sing-alongs, quirky roadside stops, and, yes, the occasional flat tire.
Extended family made everything even livelier. Grandparents, aunts, uncles—they were always dropping by, each one bringing new stories and their own lovable quirks. Holiday gatherings? Loud, a little chaotic, and always delicious, with tables practically groaning under the weight of casseroles and pies. Even when money was tight, you could feel a sense of abundance in the air.
The grown-ups shared memories of the old days, while kids plotted to sneak extra desserts or dodge dishwashing duty. And through it all, individuality had its place. Maybe there was an uncle who collected the oddest souvenirs, a cousin with a knack for magic tricks, or a grandmother who handed out advice with a mischievous wink. These little eccentricities? They weren’t just tolerated—they were celebrated.
Of course, home wasn’t perfect. There were arguments about money, worries over what tomorrow might bring, and the occasional illness to weather. But here’s the thing—those challenges were usually met with a little creativity, a good dose of patience, and sometimes, a much-needed slice of pie.
Looking back, what really stands out is the family’s ability to adapt. The world outside was changing fast, but inside those four walls, traditions stayed strong. Stories were told and retold, and the bonds of love and loyalty held firm. In a time when everything else seemed up in the air, home was the rock—a place where you belonged, no matter how quirky or ordinary you might be.

Chapter 3. School Days, Mischief, and the Power of Imagination.
Picture school in the 1950s—a world with its own rules, clear expectations, and, honestly, no shortage of opportunities for mischief. The classrooms had those old wooden desks, chalk dust hanging in the air, and that unmistakable scent of floor polish. Teachers really commanded respect, and the principal’s office? That place felt like a mix of mystery and pure dread.
Most mornings, kids would head to school buzzing with anticipation. There was the excitement of seeing friends, the challenge of new lessons, and always—always—the chance for a little adventure. Even the walk to school became an event, with groups of kids swapping stories, cracking jokes, and daring each other to do something wild. The playground? That was where the action happened—swings, jungle gyms, and high-stakes games of tag or kickball. You could almost feel the shifting alliances and silent negotiations of childhood politics.
Once inside, learning was this unique mix of memorizing facts and getting genuinely curious. Spelling bees, math drills, and history lessons filled the hours, but every now and then, someone would break the silence with a burst of laughter or a clever prank. Some kids thrived, others just tried not to nod off. But no matter where you landed, there was this feeling that everyone was in it together, sharing the ups and downs of small-town life.
But school wasn’t just about books and tests. It was a playground for the imagination. Boredom? Oh, that was the real enemy, and kids had to get creative. Maybe they’d doodle in the margins, invent secret codes, or drift off into daydreams about far-off places. The bravest found ways to push the limits—sneaking snacks, passing notes, or pulling off elaborate pranks that everyone would talk about for weeks.
There was one kid who stood out from the rest—he escaped into his own world as the Thunderbolt Kid. Whenever school felt too confining, he’d imagine himself soaring above the rooftops, outwitting the strictest teachers, even saving classmates from the grip of boredom. As the Thunderbolt Kid, he was unstoppable—fearless, clever, always just ahead of trouble.
And that imagination didn’t stop at the classroom door. After school, the neighborhood came alive. Empty lots became battlefields, backyards turned into wild jungles, and friends gathered to build forts or invent brand new games. The line between reality and make-believe blurred, and suddenly, anything seemed possible.
Of course, school had its tough moments too. Bullies, tough tests, and that constant worry about fitting in or being embarrassed—it was a lot to handle. Navigating the social scene took real skill, balancing the urge to belong with the need to stand out. Some kids struggled to find their place, but even then, there was this resilience—a quiet confidence that tomorrow could be better, that new opportunities were just around the corner.
Looking back, you realize school was so much more than just lessons and grades. It was where friendships were made, where character was shaped, and where kids learned what it meant to be loyal, creative, and persistent. Through all of it, imagination was a lifeline—turning ordinary days into unforgettable adventures, and giving every kid a chance to be extraordinary in their own way.

Chapter 4: The Joys and Oddities of American Culture in the 1950s
Let’s dive into a time when America seemed both delightfully simple and quietly complex—the 1950s.
Picture this: families gathered around the dinner table, everyone catching up on their day. Afterward, they’d all settle in front of the same flickering TV set, tuning in to black-and-white shows that made everyone laugh, dream, or just feel part of something bigger.
But, if you looked a little closer, you’d spot a world that was anything but ordinary. Underneath all that sameness, there were odd quirks, little contradictions, and even whispers of change.
Popular culture really took center stage. For most folks, television was still a new treat. Families would squeeze together on the couch, watching cowboys ride across the screen, comedians crack jokes, and variety shows bring a touch of excitement right into their living rooms. Even though the pictures were in black and white, the stories themselves were vivid and full of life. Radio was still a big deal, too—offering a mix of music, news, and those familiar voices that felt like old friends.
And then, there was the food. Imagine walking through a supermarket lined with brightly colored cereals, frozen dinners you could just pop in the oven, and instant coffee that promised to make mornings easier. Convenience foods were all the rage, but some folks still longed for the slower, homemade meals they grew up with. Diners and drive-ins popped up everywhere, serving burgers and milkshakes—a quick bite, and maybe even a little taste of freedom.
When it came to having fun, options were everywhere. Bowling alleys, roller rinks, and movie theaters were packed with people looking for a little escape. Baseball was the game everyone followed, and summer meant trips to the pool, picnics in the park, or the thrill of the county fair. It really felt like everyone was connected, part of one big community.
But American culture had its own oddities, too. Think about the advertisements of the time—they promised miracles. Whiter teeth, spotless floors, and happier families, all at the push of a button. New inventions seemed to pop up all the time, each one claiming to be the next big thing. Some stuck around, while others just faded away. There was this real fascination with the future, this sense that science and technology could fix anything.
At the same time, there were all these unspoken rules. How you should act, what you ought to wear, even what you were supposed to believe. Conformity was valued, and anyone who didn’t quite fit the mold risked being seen as odd or rebellious. Still, people found ways to show who they really were. Teenagers, especially, started pushing boundaries with new music, wild fashion, and their own slang. Parents worried—was rock and roll or those comic books going to ruin everything?
The 1950s were full of contradictions. On the outside, prosperity was everywhere—but not everyone shared in it. Issues like race, gender, and class were always there, just beneath the surface. People didn’t talk about them much, but you could feel the tension. The seeds for big social changes were already being planted, even as most folks just wanted to hold onto what felt familiar.
For kids growing up back then, all these oddities just seemed normal. The latest toy, the newest TV show, or the most popular snack—these were the things that made you feel like you belonged. But there was also this sense of wonder, like the future was wide open and anything could happen.
Looking back, it’s easy to see how the joys and oddities of the 1950s left their mark. There’s a real nostalgia for a time when life seemed simpler, even though the world was shifting in ways no one could have imagined.

Chapter 5: Friendship, Freedom, and the Unwritten Rules of Childhood
Let’s take a little trip back to the 1950s—when childhood friendships were forged through real, shared adventures. Imagine the playground, the classroom, or just the streets of your own neighborhood. Those bonds? They were tough as nails and meant to last. Back then, there was a kind of freedom that’s almost hard to picture today. Kids could roam, explore, and hey, even mess up once in a while—without someone hovering over their shoulder.
The neighborhood itself felt like its own tiny universe. Groups of kids moved together, letting the sun decide when the day would start and end. No strict schedules—just the thrill of whatever came next. There were all these unwritten rules, too—like who got to jump into a game, who’d lead the charge, and how arguments would play out. Sure, tempers flared sometimes, but just as quickly, new alliances would form and the next adventure would begin.
Friendship in those days? It was all about trust, loyalty, and a touch of mischief. Secret clubs, special handshakes, codes only your group understood—those little things meant everything. The best friends were the ones you could trust with a secret, who’d cover for you if you made a mistake, or who’d split that last, stolen cookie. Together, you faced the tough stuff: schoolyard bullies, strict teachers, and the looming threat of getting in trouble at home.
With all that freedom came some risks, of course. But without grown-ups watching every move, kids learned to figure things out themselves. They built forts, made up games, and handled arguments on their own. There were plenty of scrapes and bruises, but also this amazing sense of accomplishment. The world felt safe—yet totally filled with possibilities.
Those unwritten rules—well, they were always shifting. Kids had to navigate who was in charge, protect their reputations, and respect invisible boundaries. Some kids naturally took the lead, while others were happy following along. There was space for being yourself, but everyone still felt the pressure to fit in. The fear of being left out? Very real. But so was the pure joy of truly belonging.
When you look back, it’s clear those friendships and freedoms shaped who those kids would become as adults. The lessons—about loyalty, resilience, and just how important play really is—lasted a lifetime. Sure, the world’s changed since then. But the memories of those simple days? They stay bright, reminding us of a time when life felt so much simpler, and the possibilities stretched out endlessly ahead.

Chapter 6: The Onset of Adolescence and the Shifting Landscape
You know, adolescence rarely announces itself with a bang. It sneaks in—almost like a whisper. Maybe it’s a voice that suddenly drops a note, or that awkward feeling in your own skin. Suddenly, every conversation feels charged with a new kind of self-awareness.
In Des Moines, the world that had once felt so safe and familiar started to shift beneath the feet of kids growing up. The old games that once brought so much joy? Well, they just didn’t have the same magic anymore. Instead, there was this restless curiosity about what might be waiting just outside the neighborhood.
For one boy, being the Thunderbolt Kid began to feel a little... tight, like a favorite costume you’ve outgrown. Sure, the cape was still tucked away in a drawer, but the urge to wear it faded as bigger questions started to take over. What did it even mean to be cool? How do you talk to girls without sounding like a fool? And why did adults always seem so busy, so caught up in things that didn’t make any sense to a kid who was just starting to glimpse the bigger world?
School changed, too. Teachers seemed a bit more serious, and lessons suddenly got harder. There were new rules—some you could read, others you just had to pick up by watching. The social scene turned into a maze, with cliques forming and breaking up faster than you could keep track. Some kids shot up like weeds, while others lagged behind. The simple politics of the playground gave way to these mysterious, often confusing negotiations of growing up.
Picture this: one afternoon, a bunch of friends crammed into a basement, the air thick with popcorn and that jittery energy you feel when everyone’s trying to act a little older than they really are. Someone pulls out a deck of cards. Suddenly, everyone’s gossiping about what the older kids get up to—dances, first dates, maybe even sneaking a sip of forbidden beer. There’s laughter, a bit of bravado, and this shared sense that the world is opening up... even as it gets a whole lot more complicated.
And at home, things were changing, too. Parents seemed a little more distant, wrapped up in their own worries. Sure, family routines went on, but there was this new tension in the air—like the old certainties were slipping away. Arguments flared up more often, and those childhood rituals that used to feel so comforting sometimes just made you ache for independence.
That’s when it hits you: growing up means letting go of some things, even as new possibilities come into view. The world feels bigger, scarier, and—let’s be honest—way more exciting than ever. The Thunderbolt Kid still showed up now and then, but he wasn’t alone anymore. New dreams stepped in—dreams of adventure, of falling in love, of finding your own place in a world that was spinning faster every day.

Chapter Seven: The Winds of Change—America in Transition.
The 1960s didn’t burst onto the scene—they crept in, rumbling quietly but insistently. If you lived in Des Moines, or anywhere in the Midwest, you couldn’t help but notice that the world was shifting all around you.
News of protests, new music, even distant wars, made their way into living rooms through televisions and newspapers. That feeling of safety, the steady calm of the 1950s, began to slip away. Instead, uncertainty crept in, and people started to realize the world was way more complicated than they’d once believed.
For families in the heartland, this change was a mix of excitement and worry. Those familiar routines—family dinners, Sunday drives, afternoons at the local pool—still went on. But there was a different tone around the dinner table. Parents found themselves quietly anxious, thinking about the future, about jobs, politics, and how to keep their kids safe.
Teenagers, on the other hand, felt something stirring deep down. They wanted more—they wanted to break out of small-town life and see what was waiting for them beyond those familiar streets.
Picture this: one evening, a family gathers around the TV to catch the evening news. The screen fills with images of marches and speeches. The adults glance at each other, saying so much without a word. The kids watch, only half-interested, a little confused yet sensing that something big is happening—even if they’re not sure what it all means. Later, lying in bed, they can’t help but wonder: What’s my place in all this? How will I fit into this changing world?
Music started to mean everything. It was a lifeline, a way to feel connected to something bigger. Radios played songs about rebellion, hope, and heartbreak. Kids traded records, memorized every lyric, and formed bands in garages—hoping, maybe, to change the world themselves. The gap between the generations grew wider. Parents shook their heads at the wild new sounds—and those haircuts—while their kids dreamed of something more, something different.
Even school wasn’t the same anymore. The curriculum stretched to include new ideas, fresh perspectives, and teachers began encouraging real debate. Students started speaking up. There were arguments, protests, sometimes even walkouts. The world didn’t seem so black and white now—suddenly, there were endless shades of gray.
Looking back, it’s clear: the 1960s were a time of both loss and discovery. Childhood innocence faded, but a new sense of possibility took its place. Change wasn’t just coming—it was necessary.
Those experiences, those lessons from the past, stayed with people—even as the future called them forward.

Chapter Eight: The Bittersweet Nature of Nostalgia.
You ever notice how, as the years roll by, those childhood memories start to glow a little brighter? Suddenly, that world of the Thunderbolt Kid—with its endless summers and simple joys—turns into this magical place you visit in your dreams, or maybe share in stories with old friends.
All those quirky family routines—stuff you barely even noticed back then—now feel so precious. They’re these fragile little reminders of a time when everything just felt safe, and the world seemed… well, understandable.
Nostalgia’s funny, isn’t it? It has this way of softening the sharp edges of the past. Sometimes, it’ll even make the tough times feel sweeter, at least in hindsight. For folks who grew up back in the '50s or '60s, those memories of home—of friends, first crushes, and even heartbreak—become a kind of anchor. Something you hold onto while the world keeps on spinning and changing.
Picture this: one day, an old friend shows up in town. Pretty soon, the whole gang of former classmates is packed into a little diner. And just like that, the years start to melt away. You’re swapping stories, cracking up over ancient inside jokes, reliving the people and the places that made you who you are.
Sure, there’s a sense of loss in the air—friends who’ve moved, parents who’ve passed, dreams that didn’t quite make it. But there’s also this deep gratitude. A kind of quiet thankfulness for the years that left something lasting in your heart.
And, of course, the Thunderbolt Kid is never far from these conversations. He’s right there in every story—a symbol of the freedom and wild imagination that defined those younger days. Even now, as grown-ups, you catch yourselves slipping back into those old roles, teasing each other, remembering adventures that once felt like the center of the universe.
After a while, it hits you—nostalgia isn’t just about longing for what’s gone. It’s about making sense of who we are, and how we ended up here. Those childhood memories, with all their ups and downs, are woven right into the fabric of your life. They remind you of what you’ve lost, sure, but also of everything you still carry—every single day.

Chapter 9: The Enduring Power of Imagination
Growing up—it's all about learning to let go. But you know what? That doesn’t mean you have to stop dreaming.
Maybe the Thunderbolt Kid was just a childhood invention, but his spirit... well, it never really left. It stuck around in the choices we make, the risks we take, and those little acts of courage that sneak into everyday adult life.
Turns out, imagination isn’t something just for kids. It’s actually a tool—a way to survive, to bring meaning to a world that can feel both beautiful and a little overwhelming at times.
As the years rolled on, adult life brought its own waves—jobs to juggle, relationships to navigate, disappointments to face, and, of course, those unexpected moments of pure joy. Sure, the routines of childhood faded into new responsibilities, but the lessons we learned stuck with us.
The real magic? It’s in seeing the world with fresh eyes, finding laughter in the most ordinary moments, and holding onto the belief that things can get better. Those are gifts that never really go away.
Picture this: one afternoon, a parent stands at the window, watching their own child play in the backyard. The kid’s cape flutters in the breeze, and for a second, it’s like looking back in time—familiar and brand new all at once. It’s a powerful reminder that imagination and discovery just keep going, generation after generation.
The world might change, but our need for wonder, for adventure, for that feeling that anything’s possible—that never fades.
And really, the legacy of the Thunderbolt Kid isn’t just about wild adventures. It’s about the spirit behind them. The courage to dream, to laugh, to find joy in the simple, everyday stuff—that’s what lasts.
In a world that’s always telling us to be serious and fit in, hanging on to a little bit of playfulness? That’s a rare and precious gift.

Chapter 10: Looking Back, Moving Forward
You know, time really does have a way of slipping by, doesn’t it? Sometimes it feels like we blink, and we’re left holding memories—some sweet, some just a little bittersweet. The world of the 1950s and 60s, with all its quirks and charm, is long gone now. In its place, we’re facing new challenges, and new opportunities every single day.
But here’s something that’s never changed: the lessons we picked up along the way. The importance of family, the power of real friendship, and the magic that comes from letting our imaginations run wild. All of that? Still just as relevant today as it ever was.
When we look back, it’s pretty clear how those early experiences shaped who we became. Think about it—the routines, the little rituals, all those small acts of kindness and courage. They left a mark, didn’t they? Sure, the world may look different now, but that deep need for connection, for meaning, for a true sense of belonging... that’s something we all still crave.
As we wrap up the story of the Thunderbolt Kid, there’s this overwhelming feeling of gratitude. Gratitude for the people who stood by us, for the places that felt like home, and for those moments that made childhood feel downright magical. And you know what else? There’s hope, too—a real belief that the very best parts of our past can come with us, woven right into the fabric of our lives as we move forward.
Growing up isn’t exactly a walk in the park—it’s messy, unpredictable, sometimes even a little scary. But it’s also filled with wonder, laughter, and discovery. Sure, life might be more complicated now, but those old lessons? They still guide us, comfort us, and inspire us when we need it most.
So, here’s the key takeaway: it’s the stories we share, and the memories we hold close, that bring real meaning to our lives. And as we look ahead, those memories can light the way.

As we wrap up our journey, think about where you’ve just been. You haven’t just walked the blocks of Des Moines—you’ve wandered through the heart of a time when the world felt a little smaller, and honestly, a bit more magical.
The Life and Times of the Thunderbolt Kid isn’t just a memoir. It’s a gentle nudge to notice that the ordinary moments in life can be truly extraordinary. That even with all its quirks and contradictions, the past still has plenty to teach us.
So, what does this all mean for you?
Childhood freedom and wild imagination—they’re not just memories. They’re the foundation of the resilience and creativity you carry into adulthood. Those family quirks and routines? They’re the glue that holds us together, shaping a sense of belonging that lasts a lifetime.
Sure, the world keeps changing. Sometimes that feels uncertain, even a little scary. But every shift brings new chances for growth and discovery.
Nostalgia isn’t just looking back—it’s a way to understand where you’ve come from, and to appreciate where you are right now.
And maybe most important: imagination and humor aren’t just for kids. They’re lifelong tools—helping you find your way, even when things get complicated.
So as you think about your own story, remember—the magic of childhood isn’t gone. It’s right there with you, in the way you see the world, the chances you take, and the laughter you share.
The world is always going to shift and surprise us. But the lessons we take—kindness, curiosity, the courage to dream—those are always close by.
Let yourself remember. Let yourself imagine. And let yourself keep moving forward, with the quiet confidence that you’ve already lived through wonder. The Thunderbolt Kid lives on in each of us—every time we choose to see the world, not just as it is, but as it could be.
